item.title: Lawyers for US inmate who survived lethal injections demand release
item.description:
The failed execution of Christa Pike is not the first time Tennessee has struggled to carry out a death sentence by lethal injection, raising questions about the drug at the center of the procedure and prompting some politicians to consider alternative forms of execution. Before Pike, no inmate in the modern era of the death penalty had survived after lethal-injection drugs were administered. Seven people had previously survived failed execution attempts. In those cases, however, the executions were halted because medical officials failed to establish an IV line, according to the Death Penalty Information Center . The controversial drug — pentobarbital — has been used by states across the country and, during President Donald Trump’s first term, to carry out death sentences. It turns out you can trace America’s 2008 financial crash, in a roundabout way, to 18th-century Prussia. The Seven Years’ War left the kingdom in financial shambles: Just to afford the fighting, Prussia’s king, Frederick the Great, had hired private minters to ramp up currency production . So in 1769, Frederick the Great landed on a novel strategy to keep money flowing into his borders. He organized cash-poor nobles into cooperatives, and began offering, to the highest bidders, bonds based on the value of their land. European investors snapped them up, giving Prussia the injection of cash it needed. It was, as the journalist Robin Wigglesworth writes in his new book, A Fabulous Debt: The Epic History of How Bonds Built the Modern World , possibly the world’s first mortgage bond sale.
